meta.title: Ragon — a coding helper that runs on the machine on your desk
meta.description: Ragon is a coding helper, a chat assistant and a desktop app, and all of it runs on your own GB10. Nothing is sent to a cloud. There is no account, no bill for each use, and no tracking.

new.h201: The desktop app on a Mac, Linux and Windows
new.p02: The desktop app puts both ways of using Ragon in one window: Ask, where you put questions, and Work, where the helper edits your code. Work has a box to type tasks in (you can attach files, skills and commands), a pane to look over changes before you keep or undo them, separate working copies of your code (worktrees), terminal tabs, and a file tree beside the conversation. On your other computers the app talks to your GB10, which it finds on your network.
new.p04: The install command puts Ragon in Applications next to ragon, and you open it like any other app. It runs on Apple silicon and Intel, with macOS 12 or later. ragon update updates it.
new.p06: On the GB10, the file ragon_<version>_arm64.deb installs the app, its menu entry and the ragon-app command, along with the sandbox profile it needs. (A sandbox is a closed room for running commands, so they can't touch the rest of the machine.)
new.p07: Then open it from the application menu, or type ragon app. More.
new.p09: The PowerShell line installs the app too, for you alone and without administrator rights, with an entry in the Start menu. Settings → Apps removes it, and ragon update updates it. Smart App Control must be off.
new.p11: The release page also has the Mac disk image (Ragon-<version>-arm64-preview.dmg, or x64 for Intel) and the Windows installer (Ragon-Setup-<version>-x64.exe, or arm64). They are unsigned previews, so when you download them in a browser, your system stops them the first time. Before you open one, check it against the release's signed SHA256SUMS file.
new.li12: macOS 15 and later: drag Ragon to Applications and open it once. Then go to System Settings › Privacy & Security and press Open Anyway. On macOS 14 and earlier, Control-click the app and choose Open.
new.li13: Windows: SmartScreen › More info › Run anyway. Smart App Control must be off.
try.p02: Or leave work for tonight with /night add <task>. Ragon goes through the list while you sleep, each task on its own git branch, and you look over the branches in the morning.
proof.h201: Your code stays on your desk, and you can check that it does
proof.p02: A cloud coding helper sends your source code to computers that belong to someone else. Ragon sends it nowhere. The model runs on your GB10, and nothing in Ragon calls home: no usage counts, no measurements, no sign-in, not even "anonymous" crash reports. So you can use it on code you are not allowed to upload, such as a client's work, protected data or a product not yet released.
proof.p03: One command runs a real Ragon session under strace, a tool that watches every call a program makes, and then lists each network connection the session opened:
proof.p04: All of it stayed on 127.0.0.1, which is the machine talking to itself. There was not one DNS lookup (a DNS lookup is asking the internet for the address of a name).
proof.p06: Type /airgapped on. Every command the helper runs then gets an empty network from the Linux kernel. That is not a polite request to the model. There is simply no network to reach. At the same time, Full Access, which would get around the sandbox, is refused.
proof.p08: Only what you or the helper ask for: a web search (through a private SearXNG that runs on your own machine, though the search itself still goes out to the web), a fetch of a web page, a read-only request to a Google account you have connected, or a check for updates. With /airgapped on, none of these happens.
why.p03: The model, your code, your questions and its answers stay on the machine where they are.
why.li05: An egress audit you can run again
why.li16: No tuning: we chose the model, the memory size, the low-level code and the speculative decoding for the GB10.
why.li17: It should not freeze your machine: it checks the machine before loading the model, and watches memory while it loads.
why.li18: Your other computers find it on your network.
features.p03: It reads your project, runs commands and tests, edits code, and asks you first before anything risky.
features.p05: Type /night add <task> before bed. By morning each task is done on its own git branch. Nothing is merged or pushed unless you do it.
features.p07: Search goes through a private SearXNG on your own machine, so there is no search account and no key to get. The questions still go out to the web to be answered.
features.p09: A list of where things are defined and who uses them across your project, so the helper can look code up and not search for it by guessing.
features.p11: Skills you wrote for Claude Code, Gemini CLI, OpenClaw or Hermes work here as they are.
features.p13: Questions with web search, image search and speaking instead of typing, and your helper sessions too, from this machine or from a phone you have paired with it. It all uses the same model on your machine.
features.p15: Ask and Work in one window, on the GB10, a Mac, Linux or Windows. The helper's sessions ask your approval, and there is a pane for reviewing changes, separate working copies, and undo.
features.p17: Read-only, through a sign-in that stays on your machine. It is switched off completely with /airgapped on.

machines.p02: All of them have the same chip, the same 128 GB of memory shared by the processor and the graphics, and DGX OS 7, so one installer covers them. We develop and test Ragon every day on the ASUS Ascent GX10. The others are covered by our automated tests, but we don't run them by hand.
faq.p03: Yes, to run the model. Your other computers are clients that borrow it: Linux (Arm or x86) and macOS with the same install command, and Windows (Arm or x86, preview) with the PowerShell line.
faq.p07: Nothing for the program or for the model. Ragon is open source under the AGPL, and the model's weights are free to use. You pay for the machine and the electricity it uses.
faq.summary08: What do I need besides the machine?
faq.p09: The operating system it comes with (DGX OS 7, or Ubuntu 24.04 where NVIDIA offers it), Docker with the NVIDIA Container Toolkit, Python 3 and Git. On plain Ubuntu, ragon-admin host check tells you what is missing.
faq.summary10: Does anything ever go out to the internet?
faq.p11: Only what you or the helper ask for, such as a web search (through a SearXNG that runs on your own machine) and the downloads on first use. With /airgapped on, all of it is off.
faq.p13: Qwen3.8-27B, in NVIDIA's 4-bit format called NVFP4, served by our own engine, ragon-serve, with a small guessing helper called a DFlash2 drafter; SGLang stays as the fallback through 0.9.x. We chose and tuned all of it for the GB10. The weights take about 20 GB, and while it runs, about 38 GB of the machine's memory stays free.
cta.h201: Keep your code on your desk
cta.p02: If you think code should stay on the desk where it was written, star the repository on GitHub. That is how other GB10 owners find Ragon.

new.c1_h3: The ragon-serve engine, the ScaleSearch drafter, and a Forgejo on each node
new.c1_p: ragon-serve runs Qwen3.8-27B on the GB10 with a 262K-token memory. Every node gets its own private Forgejo (a place to keep git repositories), and the Telegram Mini App works directly on your repositories.
new.c2_h3: Host sockets closed, a local file index, and LoRA adapters
new.c2_p: Inside the command sandbox, the Docker, containerd, D-Bus and systemd sockets are closed (a socket is a door a program can use to give orders to the system). ragon-docs now reads scanned pages and office documents too, and the server can serve signed LoRA adapters (small add-ons that change what a model is good at).
new.c3_h3: The desktop app on macOS, Linux and Windows, and Night Shift best-of-N
new.c3_p: Ask and Work share one desktop window, with a review pane, worktrees and terminal tabs. /night add --best-of N runs a task N times and keeps the best try.
surfaces.r3_h3: JetBrains, VS Code, and your phone
surfaces.r3_p: You can connect JetBrains or VS Code through stdio MCP (ragon-admin mcp). You can also send messages to your GB10 from Signal (to yourself, in Note to Self), from Telegram (with the Mini App for working on repositories), and from Matrix over Tailscale. Every phone link is off until you turn it on. Signal is end-to-end encrypted, and Matrix runs on a server of your own. Telegram messages pass through Telegram's servers unencrypted, so use it only for things you would not mind sharing that way.
